newsitem.title: CANADA: Ottawa, unions battle over Canadian Airlines.
newsitem.headline: Ottawa, unions battle over Canadian Airlines.

text.p: Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said on Friday he wanted employees of the troubled Canadian Airlines Corp. to bypass their unions and vote on a tough restructuring plan proposed by the company.

"I completely agree that the employees of Canadian should have the right to vote on their future and on the restructuring programme that has been proposed by Mr. (Kevin) Benson, the (chief executive) of Canadian Airlines," Anderson told Canada's parliament.
The company's big unions quickly rejected the 10 percent wage rollbacks and called on the government to bail out Canada's second biggest carrier.
Anderson said Canadian had asked for no direct cash assistance, nor would any be given.

"We want to make sure that plan has a fair chance and I know it's difficult for the employees, but we want them to be able to vote on that plan...a government bailout does not appear to be a viable option," he said.

Calgary, Alberta-based Canadian has said it could face oblivion early in 1997 unless it enacts a strategy of wage cuts for its 16,400 employees, cuts in fees paid to 33 percent-owner AMR Corp., parent of American Airlines, and route restructurings.
Canadian's biggest union, the 5,300-member International Association of Machinists, repeated on Friday that it would not support an employee vote on Canadian's life-support plan.
"There's no movement on that," said IAM spokesman Neville Hamilton. "We have a collective agreement in place and we're showing some leadership on the issue and that's it."
Hamilton said a mechanism existed for the members to review the collective agreement, but that there had been no indication of plans to use it.
Union officials for the IAM and Canadian's 3,700 workers who belong to the Canadian Auto Workers union, have both rejected the company's wage cut demands.
Anderson told reporters after speaking in parliament that he had not checked to see if the government could force the unions to hold a vote.
Canadian has set an end-of-November deadline for participants to respond to its survival plan.
